steps.tx: **Pulmonary tuberculosis** (TB, lung infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis) is defined by airborne droplet spread with prolonged cough and systemic symptoms. India carries about 25% of global incident cases, with over 2 million new cases yearly. **Latent tuberculosis infection** (LTBI, immune control without disease) affects about 40% of adults, of whom 5 to 10% progress in lifetime. Smear positive patients drive transmission.
steps.say: Pulmonary tuberculosis is lung infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and it spreads by airborne droplets. India has about one quarter of global incident cases and it reports over two million new cases yearly. Latent infection is immune control without disease and it affects about forty percent of adults. About ten percent of latent cases progress during the lifetime. Smear positive patients are the main drivers of transmission and they can infect many contacts.

steps.tx: **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** (waxy acid fast bacillus) is the causative organism with droplet nuclei reaching alveoli. Primary infection involves **Ghon focus** (subpleural granuloma) plus hilar nodes. **Reactivation TB** (endogenous spread from dormant bacilli) follows waning immunity. Risk factors include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, tumour necrosis factor inhibitor use, silicosis, HIV infection, undernutrition and prior tuberculosis treated incompletely. Household contact increases risk.
steps.say: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a waxy acid fast bacillus and it is the cause of tuberculosis. Primary infection forms a Ghon focus with hilar nodes in the lung and it is localised. Reactivation disease is endogenous spread from dormant bacilli when immunity falls and it is dangerous. Risk factors are diabetes, chronic kidney disease, silicosis, HIV infection and undernutrition. Household contact increases risk and it is a strong predictor of infection. Clinicians should ask every patient with chronic symptoms about contacts and they must remain vigilant.

steps.tx: **Delayed type hypersensitivity** (cell mediated immunity) limits bacilli within **granuloma** (organised macrophage cluster) with caseous necrosis at centre. Fibrosis walls off lesions but hypoxic caseum harbours dormant bacilli. When immunity wanes, caseum liquefies and bacilli multiply, causing **cavitation** (air filled cavity) and bronchogenic spread. This explains lower lobe healing in primary disease and upper lobe reactivation near high oxygen tension.
steps.say: Granuloma formation is a cell mediated immune response and it limits bacilli within macrophages. Caseous necrosis at the centre creates a haven for dormant bacilli and it is characteristic. Fibrosis is a wall that contains lesions and hypoxic caseum preserves viable organisms for years. When immunity wanes, caseum liquefies and bacilli multiply rapidly and disease spreads. Cavitation follows and it causes bronchogenic spread to other lobes. This mechanism explains the upper lobe predilection seen in reactivation disease and it is classic.

steps.tx: Classic history is **prolonged cough** (more than 2 to 3 weeks) with **haemoptysis** (blood in sputum), **evening fever** (low grade) and **night sweats** (drenching). **Weight loss** (cachexia) and loss of appetite complete the syndrome. Examination shows apical crepitations, amphoric breathing over a cavity and localised dullness. **Clubbing** (nail bed change) and lymphadenopathy may appear. Primary TB in adults often is subclinical, while reactivation presents classically.
steps.say: Classic history is prolonged cough beyond two to three weeks with haemoptysis and blood in sputum. Evening fever and drenching night sweats are common systemic features. Weight loss and loss of appetite complete the syndrome and they indicate chronic disease. Examination reveals apical crepitations and amphoric breathing over a cavity. Clubbing and lymphadenopathy may be present and they should be sought carefully. Primary disease in adults is often subclinical and reactivation is classic.

steps.tx: **Sputum smear for acid fast bacilli** (AFB, Ziehl Neelsen stain) is first test, with **sputum culture** (Löwenstein Jensen or MGIT liquid) as sensitive gold standard though slow. **GeneXpert MTB RIF** (Xpert cartridge assay) detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within 2 hours. **Chest radiography** (X ray) shows upper lobe infiltrate, cavitation, fibrosis or miliary nodular pattern. **Basal sputum induction** helps smear negative cases. **Bronchoscopy** adds lavage when sputum is non diagnostic.
steps.say: Sputum smear for acid fast bacilli is the first test and it is rapid but insensitive. Sputum culture is the sensitive gold standard but it is slow and can take weeks. GeneXpert assay is a rapid test and it detects tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within two hours. Chest radiography is classic and it shows upper lobe infiltrate, cavitation or miliary nodular pattern. Sputum induction helps when smear is negative. Bronchoscopy adds lavage when sputum remains non diagnostic and it can improve yield.

steps.tx: National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme **NTEP regimen** (8 to 12 month standard) uses **isoniazid** 300 mg daily, **rifampicin** 600 mg daily, **pyrazinamide** 1000 to 1500 mg daily and **ethambutol** 1000 to 1500 mg daily for 2 months intensive phase. **Streptomycin** is no longer routine. Daily dosing is preferred over intermittent. Weight band dosing applies. **Pyridoxine** 50 mg daily prevents isoniazid neuropathy.
steps.say: NTEP treatment uses isoniazid three hundred milligrams daily and it is a core drug. Rifampicin is six hundred milligrams daily and it is essential for sterilisation. Pyrazinamide is one thousand to one thousand five hundred milligrams daily and ethambutol is similar. The intensive phase is two months and daily dosing is preferred over intermittent. Weight band dosing is required for children and adults. Pyridoxine fifty milligrams daily prevents isoniazid neuropathy and it is given routinely.

steps.tx: **WHO 2022 guidelines** (World Health Organization) endorse 6-month **BPaL or BPaLM regimens** (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid with or without moxifloxacin) for drug resistant tuberculosis. **Drug sensitive TB** remains 4 to 6 months with **BDQ 6 month** extension for severe disease. **Miliary TB** (disseminated) needs at least 9 to 12 months. **TB meningitis** needs at least 9 to 12 months with steroids. **Drug susceptibility testing** (DST, culture sensitivity) guides changes. **Contact tracing** is mandatory.
steps.say: WHO twenty twenty two guidelines are the standard and they endorse six month BPaL regimens for drug resistant tuberculosis. BPaL is bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid with or without moxifloxacin and it is all oral. Drug sensitive disease is treated for four to six months and daily therapy is standard. Miliary tuberculosis needs at least nine to twelve months and it is disseminated disease. TB meningitis needs at least nine to twelve months with adjunctive steroids. Drug susceptibility testing guides changes and contact tracing is mandatory.

steps.tx: Complications include **haemoptysis** (massive bleeding from Rasmussen aneurysm) and **pneumothorax** (air leak from cavitation). **Bronchiectasis** (dilated bronchi) and **fibrosis** (scarring) cause chronic respiratory failure. **Cor pulmonale** (right heart failure) follows vascular pruning. **Disseminated TB** (miliary, meningeal, bone, genitourinary) carries higher mortality. Adverse effects include **hepatotoxicity** (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) and **optic neuritis** (ethambutol). Most drug sensitive disease is curable with adherence above 90%.
steps.say: Complications include massive haemoptysis from Rasmussen aneurysm and it can be fatal. Pneumothorax follows cavitation and it needs urgent care. Bronchiectasis and fibrosis cause chronic respiratory failure. Cor pulmonale is right heart failure due to vascular pruning. Disseminated disease has higher mortality than localised disease. Hepatotoxicity is common with isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide. Optic neuritis is seen with ethambutol and vision must be monitored.

steps.tx: Examiners test difference between **primary TB** (lower lobe, hilar nodes, often subclinical) and **post primary TB** (upper lobe cavity, smear positive). **Miliary TB** (millet seeds, miliary nodular pattern) is a different entity from **non tuberculosis mycobacteria** disease requiring longer therapy. **Pott disease** (spine TB) and **TB meningitis** (basal exudate) are extrapulmonary forms that are tested. **Mantoux test** (tuberculin skin) has limited value in endemic BCG vaccinated populations and it is not diagnostic alone.
steps.say: Examiners test the difference between primary and post primary tuberculosis and it is important. Primary disease is lower lobe with hilar nodes and it is often subclinical. Post primary disease is upper lobe cavitary and it is smear positive. Miliary disease is disseminated millet seed pattern and it is distinct. Non tuberculosis mycobacteria need prolonged therapy and they are different organisms. Mantoux test has limited value in endemic areas and it is not diagnostic alone.

steps.tx: **Contact investigation** (household screening) identifies active cases and **latent infection** needs treatment with **isoniazid preventive therapy** (IPT, 300 mg (10 mg/kg) daily for 6 months) or **rifampicin** 4 months. **HIV testing** is mandatory for all TB patients. **Directly observed therapy** (DOT, short course observed dosing) improves adherence but is now video supported. ** Nikshay portal** (national notification system) tracks every case and is legally mandatory for notification.
steps.say: Contact investigation is household screening and it identifies active cases early. Latent infection needs treatment with isoniazid preventive therapy for six months. Rifampicin for four months is an alternative and it is preferred in some settings. HIV testing is mandatory for all patients and it changes management. Directly observed therapy improves adherence but video support is now used. Nikshay portal is the national notification system and it is legally mandatory for every case.

steps.tx: High yield patterns are prolonged cough, upper lobe cavity, smear positive disease and miliary pattern. Remember daily NTEP dosing, GeneXpert for resistance and culture as gold standard. **INH**, **RIF**, **PZA**, **ETB** are core 4 drugs. BPaL is for resistant disease and meningitis needs steroids. steps.say: High yield patterns include prolonged cough, upper lobe cavity, smear positive disease and miliary pattern. Clinicians should remember daily NTEP dosing and GeneXpert for resistance. Sputum culture is the gold standard and it is sensitive but slow. Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol are core drugs and they are essential. BPaL is for resistant disease and meningitis needs steroids. The table below collects drugs, doses, durations and gold tests for quick revision.
